name: x86-simd-sort (numpy/x86-simd-sort)
workload: Sorting an array of custom C++ Point structs (3D float/double coordinates) via object_qsort vs std::sort, sorted by one coordinate, Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance, or Chebyshev distance, measured with Google Benchmark on an AVX-512 capable processor.
claimed_speedup: object_qsort up to 5x faster for 32-bit key type and about 4x for 64-bit key type when sorting by one struct member; up to 10x faster when sorting by Euclidean distance
hardware: unspecified x86 processor with AVX-512 support
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; used as a submodule by NumPy (np.sort/argsort/partition) and PyTorch (torch.sort), integrated into OpenJDK, used by Alibaba GRAPE and OceanBase
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 or AVX2; object_qsort needs O(N) extra memory for key/index arrays; speedup is highly dependent on the struct/key definition, README itself recommends benchmarking per use case rather than assuming the headline numbers.
caveats: README does not state the exact CPU model or compiler flags used for the object_qsort chart, only 'a processor with AVX-512'. Numbers come from the project's own README, not an independent third party.
found_via: GitHub/web search 'SIMD sort faster than std::sort' and 'x86-simd-sort Intel AVX-512 quicksort faster than std::sort'; confirmed via gh api repo metadata and a direct read of README.md and src/README.md

name: IPS4o (In-place Parallel Super Scalar Samplesort)
workload: Sequential and parallel sorting of up to 2^32 64-bit floating point elements across 9 input distributions (Uniform, Exponential, AlmostSorted, RootDup, TwoDup, EightDup, Sorted, ReverseSorted, Ones) and several data types, run on multiple multi-core Intel/AMD machines, compared against GCC's std::sort ('std-sort'), DualPivot quicksort, BlockQuicksort, and s3-sort.
claimed_speedup: DualPivot and std-sort, which do not avoid branch mispredictions, are at least a factor of 1.86 slower than IS4o (sequential) for n = 2^32; IPS4o also outperforms the best in-place parallel comparison-based competitor by up to a factor of 3
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2683 v4 16-core dual-socket ('Intel2S'), Intel Xeon E5-4640 8-core quad-socket ('Intel4S'), AMD Ryzen 1800X 8-core ('AMD1S'); 512 GiB RAM on the Intel machines, 32 GiB on AMD1S
stars_or_usage: 135 stars on the current org repo, 167 on the original author repo; used in the vg genome-graph toolkit
tradeoffs: Requires C++14; parallel path needs a CPU with 16-byte compare-and-exchange support (or GCC libatomic); does not compile on Windows; unstable sort (element order among equal keys is not preserved).
caveats: The paper cites its implementation at github.com/SaschaWitt/ips4o; that repository's README now says it is deprecated in favor of github.com/ips4o/ips4o, even though GitHub's own metadata records ips4o/ips4o as a fork of it. Treated ips4o/ips4o as canonical per the maintainers' own redirect notice; original repo recorded in is_fork_of.
found_via: Google Scholar/arXiv search 'ips4o in-place parallel super scalar samplesort benchmark std::sort'; paper opened and read at arxiv.org/pdf/1705.02257 (Sections 4.7 and 5, pages 8-9)

name: quadsort
workload: Sorting arrays of 32-bit integers ranging from 4 to 1024 elements, random order with weighted repetitions, using the author's wolfsort benchmark harness compiled with g++ -O3.
claimed_speedup: quadsort roughly 2.4x-5x faster than g++ libstdc++ std::stable_sort at small sizes, e.g. 4 items: 0.001189s vs 0.005899s average (~5.0x); 32 items: 0.003258s vs 0.007885s average (~2.4x)
hardware: WSL 2, gcc 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Stable but not in-place: uses O(n) swap memory by default, falls back to in-place rotations (O(n log^2 n) moves) if allocation fails; plain C, needs a template wrapper for generic C++ use.
caveats: Benchmark hardware is only described as 'WSL 2'; no CPU model given, which caps this at Tier B rather than A. Benchmarked via the author's own wolfsort harness, not an independent third party.
found_via: Web search 'fluxsort crumsort quadsort benchmark std::sort libstdc++'; opened and read scandum/quadsort README.md directly

name: fluxsort
workload: Sorting 100,000 elements of 32/64/128-byte types across multiple distributions (random order, low-cardinality 'random % 100', ascending/descending, pipe organ, random tail/half, bit reversal), using the wolfsort benchmark harness compiled with g++ -O3.
claimed_speedup: ~3.2x faster than g++ std::stable_sort on 100k random 32-bit ints (0.001890s vs 0.006068s average); ~5.6x on low-cardinality data ('random % 100'); up to ~16x on adaptive patterns such as ascending order (0.000045s vs 0.000733s average)
hardware: WSL 2, gcc 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Stable, partially in-place (swap memory scales from O(1) to O(n) depending on the partition); its branchless-partition and pivot-retention optimizations were later reused by crumsort and, per the project's own docs, by Rust's glidesort, ipnsort, and driftsort.
caveats: The benchmark table showing fluxsort vs std::stable_sort actually lives in the sibling quadsort repository's README (both use the same wolfsort harness), not in fluxsort's own README. CPU model unstated, only 'WSL 2' + gcc version, so capped at Tier B.
found_via: Web search 'fluxsort crumsort quadsort benchmark std::sort libstdc++'; opened and read scandum/fluxsort README.md and scandum/quadsort README.md (which hosts the comparison table) directly

name: Boost.Sort spreadsort
workload: Sorting arrays of integers, floats, and strings of varying sizes with Boost's spreadsort (hybrid radix/comparison sort), compared to std::sort on a Windows/MSVC machine and a separate Ubuntu/x86 machine.
claimed_speedup: integer_sort tends to be 50% to 2x faster than std::sort; float_sort and string_sort are roughly 2x faster than std::sort; integer_sort starts winning at about 1000 elements (4000 bytes), string_sort at as few as 30 strings
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 8.0 for the original Windows benchmark; unspecified gcc version for the Ubuntu follow-up
hardware: Core 2 Duo laptop running Windows Vista 64 (original benchmark); unspecified 'newer x86 system running Ubuntu' (follow-up, std::sort fallback disabled)
stars_or_usage: 58 stars on the standalone GitHub mirror; ships as part of the Boost C++ Libraries, one of the most widely deployed C++ library collections
tradeoffs: Falls back to std::sort automatically below about 1000 elements so there is no regression on small inputs; can be slower than std::sort on already reverse-sorted data; header-only, requires only a C++11 compiler.
caveats: Official benchmark hardware is old (Core 2 Duo / Windows Vista) and the 'newer x86 Ubuntu' run states no CPU model or compiler version; numbers are from Boost's own documentation, not independently reproduced in this session, and have not been updated to reflect modern CPUs.
found_via: Web search 'boost spreadsort benchmark speedup std::sort integer float'; opened boost.org official docs page and boostorg/sort repository (README.md and root file listing) directly

name: LearnedSort
workload: Sorting 50 million double-precision keys drawn from 8 distributions (Uniform, Exponential, Mixture of Gaussians, Zipf 0.75, TwoDups, Sorted, ReverseSorted, Identical), measured with Google Benchmark, comparing LearnedSort (a CDF-model-based sort) against std::sort, SkaSort, IS4o, BlockQuicksort, and Radix Sort.
claimed_speedup: Approximately 4.3x faster than GCC std::sort on Uniform data (~1150ms vs ~5000ms) and similarly ~4x on Exponential/Gaussian/Zipf/TwoDups distributions; roughly 15-20x faster on Sorted/ReverseSorted/Identical data (~50-60ms vs ~750-1000ms), per the README's bar chart
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6150 CPU @ 2.70GHz, 376GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 (kernel 5.4.0-26-generic)
stars_or_usage: 81 stars; published as 'The Case for a Learned Sorting Algorithm', SIGMOD 2020
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 is a heavier copyleft obligation than most sort peers here; only supports numeric keys without payloads or string keys per the README's stated Limitations; training the CDF model adds setup cost that is not amortized on small inputs.
caveats: The README states no benchmark numbers in text; the speedups above were read directly off the bar-chart image (plots/perf_charts.png) that is the actual evidence artifact, so they are visual estimates rather than exact printed figures. No commits since 2021; this is an unmaintained academic research prototype.
found_via: Web search 'SIMD sort faster than std::sort' / 'Learned Sort Kristo Kraska speedup std::sort benchmark'; opened anikristo/LearnedSort README.md and downloaded+viewed plots/perf_charts.png directly
